wildfireFund.title: Wildfire Fund asset and claims liability
wildfireFund.content:
AB 1054 (2019) and SB 254 (2025) created a statewide Wildfire Fund that California's large electric utilities pay into and can draw on to pay catastrophic wildfire-liability claims, capped per incident, instead of absorbing them directly. The claims liability is what PG&E still owes on pre-2019 wildfires that pushed it into Chapter 11.

For PG&E Corporation: this pair is the balance-sheet overhang the 2019 bankruptcy was about. The fund asset has been drawing down since FY2022 as it absorbs claims, while SB 254 added a mechanism to replenish it with ratepayer-backed securitization bonds -- the fund is not self-sustaining on utility contributions alone.

What to watch:

  • Fund asset falling toward zero faster than claims liability falls
  • New legislation or CPUC decisions changing the fund's replenishment terms
  • A new catastrophic wildfire year that draws the fund down sharply

customersDeliveries.title: Customers and delivery volumes
customersDeliveries.content:
Electric and gas customers are metered connections; electric deliveries is total GWh sold, the volume side of regulated revenue.

For PG&E Corporation: customer counts grow slowly (California's largest investor-owned utility, mature service territory) while deliveries have trended down -- efficiency, rooftop solar and mild weather years all cut volume even as the customer base grows. Because revenue is set by the CPUC's authorized revenue requirement, not by volume sold, falling deliveries do not translate directly into falling revenue the way they would for an unregulated seller.

What to watch:

  • Customer growth as a slow-moving proxy for rate-base growth
  • Deliveries decoupling further from revenue (decoupling is the point of rate regulation, but a widening gap is worth understanding)

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by segment
segmentRevenue.content:
PG&E's utility revenue splits between its electric and gas businesses, each with its own General Rate Case and authorized revenue requirement.

For PG&E Corporation: electric is roughly three-quarters of utility revenue and carries almost all of the wildfire-mitigation capital program, so it is the segment driving rate-base growth (and rate increases) over the next several GRC cycles; gas is smaller and more stable.

What to watch:

  • Electric revenue growth tracking the GRC rate-base buildout
  • Gas segment share shrinking as electrification policy proceeds

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For PG&E Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For PG&E Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For PG&E Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For PG&E Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For PG&E Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For PG&E Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For PG&E Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For PG&E Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For PG&E Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
